title: A Loan Can Become Higher-Priced After It Is Locked: Re-Testing HPML Status at Every Change, and What Follows When It Flips
summary: Whether a mortgage is a higher-priced mortgage loan under Regulation Z 1026.35 depends on the APR, the average prime offer rate for the week the rate was set, and the loan's lien and size. A relock, a pricing exception or a fee change can move a loan across the line after the escrow waiver and the appraisal order were already decided. A technical account of how our agents compute HPML status, when they re-test it, and the escrow, appraisal and flipped-property consequences they check before closing.
body_markdown:
## Who This Is For


Compliance officers, closing and disclosure leads, and pre-funding QC managers at lenders with a non-QM, jumbo or second-lien book, or a lock desk that grants relocks and exceptions. Also model risk teams who want to know which fields an agent's HPML determination depends on.


## A Status, Computed From Moving Parts


[Regulation Z at 12 CFR 1026.35](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/35/) defines a higher-priced mortgage loan as a closed-end consumer credit transaction secured by the consumer's principal dwelling with an annual percentage rate that exceeds the average prime offer rate for a comparable transaction, as of the date the interest rate is set, by 1.5 percentage points or more for a first lien, 2.5 points or more for a first lien above the conforming loan limit, or 3.5 points or more for a subordinate lien. HELOCs are open-end and outside the definition, and reverse mortgages, construction-only loans and a few others are excluded.


Every input to that test can move during origination. The APR changes when fees, rate or term change. The APOR comes from the weekly tables the CFPB publishes through the FFIEC, and which week applies depends on the date the rate was set, which the commentary treats as the date of the last rate lock before consummation. A relock in a different week picks up a different APOR. The comparable transaction depends on the loan's structure, a 30-year fixed or a 7-year ARM, so a product change changes the APOR row. And the threshold depends on lien position and whether the loan amount exceeds the conforming limit for the year.


So HPML is a computed status with five inputs, any of which can change after the file has been set up around the first answer.


## What the Status Changes


If the loan is an HPML, three sets of requirements apply.


The escrow rule, at 1026.35(b), requires an escrow account for property taxes and required insurance on a first-lien HPML, kept for at least five years, after which the borrower can ask to cancel it only if the unpaid principal balance is below 80% of the original value and the borrower is not delinquent or in default. Certain small creditors operating in rural or underserved areas, and since 2021 certain small insured depository institutions and credit unions, are exempt.


The appraisal rule, at 1026.35(c), requires a written appraisal by a state-certified or licensed appraiser who physically visits the interior of the property, a disclosure within three business days of application telling the borrower about the appraisal and their right to a copy, and a copy of every appraisal delivered at least three business days before consummation. The appraisal rule has its own exemptions, and the largest is that qualified mortgages are exempt. Most agency loans are QMs, so in practice the HPML appraisal rule falls mainly on non-QM, some jumbo and some portfolio loans, which is the part of the book where lenders have the fewest automated controls.


The flipped-property rule, at 1026.35(c)(4), requires a second appraisal from a different appraiser when the seller acquired the property within 90 days of the consumer's purchase agreement and the price exceeds the seller's acquisition price by more than 10%, or within 91 to 180 days and by more than 20%. The creditor cannot charge the borrower for the second appraisal. There is a list of exempt sellers and situations, including sales by a lender that acquired the property through foreclosure, sales by an estate and employee relocation sales, among others. The[CFPB's HPML appraisal rule guide](https://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/201401_cfpb_tila-hpml_appraisal-rule-guide.pdf) walks through each exemption.


There is also a status effect on QM itself. Under[1026.43(e)](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/43/) , a first-lien QM priced at or above APOR plus 1.5 points gets a rebuttable presumption of compliance with the ability-to-repay rule instead of a safe harbor. Our post on[ability-to-repay and QM](https://www.seiright.com/blog/reg-z-1026-43-ability-to-repay-qualified-mortgage-ai-underwriting) covers that line, which uses the same APOR comparison.


## How the Status Flips Late


Consider a non-QM first-lien loan, with illustrative numbers. At lock, the APR is 7.68% and the APOR for that week's comparable transaction is 6.30%, a spread of 1.38 points. Not an HPML. The loan officer grants the borrower an escrow waiver, which the lender's policy allows, and the appraisal is ordered as a standard product.


Three weeks later the lock expires before closing and the loan is relocked. The rate is the same, but the relock costs the borrower a fee, which raises the APR to 7.74%, and the APOR in the relock week is 6.21%. The spread is now 1.53 points. The loan is an HPML.


Several things are now wrong. The escrow waiver is no longer permitted, so the Closing Disclosure needs escrow payments and an initial escrow deposit, and the projected payments table changes. Here the APR moved 0.06 points, inside the one-eighth point tolerance for a regular transaction in 1026.22, so the corrected Closing Disclosure does not restart the three-business-day wait under 1026.19(f)(2)(ii); a larger relock fee would have. The HPML appraisal disclosure was never sent, because nobody thought the loan would be higher-priced. And if the seller bought the property 70 days before the borrower signed the contract at a price 15% lower, a second appraisal is now required, at the lender's cost, and the closing date is no longer realistic.


Each of these is a finding if it is missed. Together they explain why the HPML test cannot be run once at application.


## When Our Agents Re-Test


The HPML determination sits in the[Loan Graph](https://www.seiright.com/platform/loan-graph) as a derived field with its inputs recorded beside it: the APR and the disclosure it came from, the rate-set date, the APOR table week and row, the lien position, the loan amount against the conforming limit, and the exclusion and exemption checks. Because it is derived, it is recomputed whenever any input changes, and the[Orchestrator](https://www.seiright.com/how-it-works) treats a change in the result as an event that re-plans the work downstream.


In practice the re-test runs on a lock, relock or extension, a product or term change, any fee change that moves the APR, and every redisclosure, because[TRID & Cure Management](https://www.seiright.com/for-lenders/trid-and-cure-management) already recomputes the APR on each one. The APOR tables are loaded each week into the[Rulebook](https://www.seiright.com/how-it-works#rulebook) with their publication date, so a determination always cites the table version it used.


When the status flips into HPML, the agent does not quietly change the loan. It raises named items. The escrow waiver goes to the closing team with the rule. The appraisal is checked against 1026.35(c)(3), interior inspection and appraiser credential, and the appraisal disclosure gap is flagged for the compliance officer, because a late disclosure is a decision about remediation, not something an agent should paper over. The flipped-property check runs.


## The Flipped-Property Check Needs Two Documents


The flip test needs the seller's acquisition date and price, and neither is on the purchase contract. They come from the appraisal's prior sales history for the subject property and from the title commitment's vesting deed. Those two sources sometimes disagree, usually because one shows the recorded date and the other shows the contract date of the seller's purchase, and the difference can move a sale across the 90-day or 180-day line.


The[Pre-Close QC Agent](https://www.seiright.com/for-lenders/pre-close-qc-agent) reads both, and the purchase agreement's date, and computes the elapsed days and price change from each source. If both sources put the sale inside a flip window, it checks for the second appraisal and confirms no charge for it appears on the Closing Disclosure. If they disagree on which side of the line the sale falls, it does not choose. The disagreement goes to a reviewer with both documents and the dates. Our post on the[title commitment and pre-close QC](https://www.seiright.com/blog/pre-close-qc-title-commitment-hazard-insurance-review-ai-fannie-b7-2-b7-3) covers the vesting checks, and our post on[appraisal fraud and property flipping](https://www.seiright.com/blog/appraisal-fraud-property-flipping-fha-anti-flipping-rule-detection) covers FHA's separate anti-flipping rule, which has its own 90-day and 180-day windows and applies whether or not the loan is higher-priced.


In the[pre-close QC deployment at Better Mortgage](https://www.seiright.com/case-study/sei-x-nasdaq-lender) , the agent reads more than twenty document types across Conventional, FHA, VA and HELOC files, and human review per loan file fell from 4 hours 50 minutes to 47 minutes. Cross-document date checks like this one are the work that time used to go into, and the kind a reviewer under deadline is most likely to skip.


## What Gets Handed to a Person


The agent computes and re-computes the status, cites every input, and raises the consequences. It does not grant or revoke an escrow waiver, decide how to remediate a missed HPML appraisal disclosure, or decide whether to delay closing for a second appraisal. Those decisions go to the closing team and the compliance officer with the before-and-after spread, the event that moved it, and the rules that now apply. The[Evidence Trail](https://www.seiright.com/how-it-works#evidence-trail) keeps each determination, so an examiner testing a sample of non-QM loans can see what the status was on each date and why.


The rule itself has barely changed since 2014. The way loans become HPMLs late, through relocks and fee changes on files already set up, has not changed either, and it is the part that needs a test on every change rather than one at the start.
